lessons.title: Causes and types of soil erosion
lessons.html:
Why erosion matters

Topsoil holds most of the organic matter, nutrients and soil life. It forms extremely slowly, yet a single heavy thunderstorm on bare, overgrazed land can wash away years of it. South Africa has large areas affected by sheet and gully erosion, especially in parts of the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo. Silt from eroded land also fills dams and lowers water quality downstream.

Agents of erosion

  • Water erosion: raindrop impact loosens bare soil, then runoff carries it away.
  • Wind erosion: dry, loose, sandy soils in the western and central regions blow away when cover is removed.

Types of water erosion

TypeDescription
SplashRaindrops detach soil particles
SheetThin, even layer removed; often unnoticed until roots and stones show
RillSmall channels that can be ploughed out
Gully (dongas)Deep channels that cannot be crossed by implements and keep cutting back

Underlying causes

Erosion is usually a management problem: overgrazing and trampling near water points and kraals, ploughing up and down slopes, cultivating steep or erodible land, burning at the wrong time, tracks and roads that channel water, and removing riparian vegetation. Dispersive (sodic) soils are particularly prone to gully and tunnel erosion.

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 places responsibilities on land users to protect soil, vegetation and water resources, including controlling erosion. Managers should know the regulations that apply to their land and get advice from the provincial Department of Agriculture on approved conservation works.

lessons.title: Preventing erosion on cropland and veld
lessons.html:
Keep the soil covered and slow the water

Prevention is far cheaper than repairing a donga. The two principles are: keep the soil covered, and stop water from gaining speed.

On cropland

  • Contour farming: plough and plant across the slope, not up and down.
  • Contour banks and waterways: banks across the slope lead runoff at a gentle gradient into grassed waterways that carry it safely away. These must be designed and pegged correctly.
  • Conservation agriculture: minimum or no tillage, permanent soil cover with residues or cover crops, and crop rotation. This increases infiltration and organic matter.
  • Strip cropping and windbreaks to reduce wind erosion on sandy soils.
  • Keep steep and highly erodible land under permanent grass or trees.

On veld and pastures

  • Set stocking rates to carrying capacity and rest camps so the grass can recover.
  • Move water points, licks and feeding sites regularly to avoid bare patches.
  • Burn only according to a fire plan and when needed for veld management, never just before heavy rain on steep slopes.
  • Fence off and rehabilitate eroded patches; protect riverbanks.

Farm roads and tracks

Badly placed roads cause much erosion. Lay them along contours where possible and use mitre drains or humps to turn water off the road into stable, vegetated areas at regular intervals.

Monitor with fixed-point photographs at the same places each season. A ground cover estimate, simple to do on foot, shows whether management is improving the soil surface.

lessons.title: Rehabilitating gullies and planning control
lessons.html:
Repairing erosion damage

A gully keeps cutting upwards (headcut) and sideways until the cause is dealt with. Start at the catchment, not the gully: reduce runoff above it, then stabilise the channel.

Gully control steps

  1. Divert or slow water above the headcut with diversion banks or spreading the flow over grassed land.
  2. Stabilise the headcut by shaping it to a gentler slope and protecting it with stone, gabions or brush.
  3. Build check structures in the channel (stone packs, brush packs, gabions) to trap silt and slow the flow. Space them so the top of one is level with the base of the next.
  4. Revegetate with suitable grasses, using brush packing to protect seedlings.
  5. Exclude livestock until vegetation is established.

Large structures such as gabion weirs need an engineer or conservation officer's design. Poorly built structures can fail in the first flood and make erosion worse.

Planning and costing

An erosion control plan includes a farm map showing slopes, soils, waterways, eroded areas and priority sites; the measures chosen; labour, materials and cost in ZAR; a timetable that completes work before the rainy season; and a monitoring schedule. Government landcare and community programmes sometimes assist with rehabilitation; ask your local extension office.

Safety

Gully edges can collapse without warning. Do not stand on undercut edges, and take care lifting stones and handling wire for gabions; wear gloves and safety boots.

Key points

  • Erosion is mostly caused by poor cover and fast runoff, usually from management choices.
  • Keep soil covered and work across the slope.
  • Control gullies from the catchment down, then stabilise and revegetate.
  • Large structures need professional design.
  • CARA (Act 43 of 1983) requires land users to protect soil and vegetation.
